Inpatient/ Outpatient ## BLOOD CULTURE POSITIVE FOR COAGULASE NEGATIVE STAPHYLOCOCCI (CNS)
CNS are the most common contaminants isolated from blood cultures. When CNS isolated from blood cultures represent true bacteremia, the blood is usually obtained from a patient with plastic or metal in the body. The most common source of coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia is an infected intravascular catheter.
When CNS are isolated from blood, the physician should carefully assess the patient to decide whether the isolation represents disease or colonization.
Colonization is more likely if a single bottle is positive or both bottles from a single blood draw are positive. If multiple bottles are positive from separate blood draws, it is more likely that the isolates reflect disease or colonization of an intravascular device. Isolates from contaminated bottles often take several days to become positive. If the patient has risk factors for true coagulase negative staphylococcal bacteremia, catheter-related blood stream infection and/or the patient is severely ill, antimicrobials should be given (see below). If there is a plastic or metal prosthesis in the body, the physician should evaluate the site for possible infection. If the isolates are likely to represent contamination and the patient does not seem ill with CNS, antimicrobial therapy would not be helpful and should not be given.
